title: A Later Test Set Is Not a New Domain: Pretraining Familiarity Survives a Contamination-Free Hold-Out

primary_sources.paraphrase: arXiv record, v1 of 9 Sep 2026 (cs.LG). The abstract reports 13 forecasters on 7 groups from 5 domains, all test observations dated after the last model release: pretrained models win 5 groups, lose one to Theta and tie seasonal naive on exchange rates; the advantage follows how much of a domain is in the pretraining corpus, not seasonal strength or spectral entropy.

Full text. One forecast origin (1 Jan 2026); horizons 14 daily, 13 weekly, 8 monthly, 48 hourly steps; hourly context capped at 2,016 points; all models univariate. Six pretrained checkpoints including chronos-2, timesfm-2.5 and timesfm-3.0. Electricity is 46 hourly Danish grid series, where Theta ranks first. Tables of MASE, ranks, quantile loss, coverage and cost.

Authors' repository, linked from the paper: fetchers, harness, scripts, paper source and results; MIT licence for the code, no data redistributed; 17 commits from 7 to 9 Sep 2026, head 8dedc34, no tags or releases. The README still describes an older M4/M3/Tourism benchmark rather than the 2026 hold-out.

Results directory listing: a holdout_2026 folder with metrics and significance folders, data manifests, timing and two determinism files, last changed 8 Sep 2026. The files themselves were not opened.

Model card of the central model: TimesFM 3.0 PyTorch weights under the TimesFM Non-Commercial License v1.0; pretraining data listed as GiftEvalPretrain (minus sets overlapping fev-bench) and Wikipedia pageviews up to Nov 2023. The repository's commit history dates the weights upload to 2026-08-24 22:41 UTC.

claims.text: On a hold-out with one origin at 1 Jan 2026, pretrained models win 5 of 7 groups, lose one (electricity) to Theta, and are indistinguishable from every other method on daily exchange rates.
claims.metric: groups won by a pretrained model, of 7
claims.dataset: Wikipedia pageviews (daily, weekly, monthly), ERA5 weather, CAMS air quality, Danish electricity, ECB exchange rates
claims.horizon: 14 days, 13 weeks, 8 months, 48 hours, by frequency
claims.baseline: SeasonalNaive, Theta, AutoETS, AutoARIMA; LightGBM, LSTM, N-BEATS trained per dataset

claims.text: The largest gain is on weekly Wikipedia pageviews: the best pretrained model (TimesFM 3, mean MASE 1.073) is 28.4% below the best classical method (Theta, 1.499).
claims.metric: mean MASE reduction, best pretrained vs best classical (%)

claims.text: Ranked among the six pretrained models on the same series, the TimesFM family sits 0.53 ranks ahead of the Chronos family on Wikipedia (1,500 series).
claims.metric: mean rank difference, TimesFM family minus Chronos family
claims.dataset: Wikipedia pageviews, daily, weekly and monthly groups pooled
claims.baseline: Chronos family (Chronos-Bolt small and base, Chronos-2)

claims.text: On the other four domains (754 series) the same difference is 0.09 ranks; the contrast has Mann-Whitney p below 1e-5 and a rank-biserial correlation of -0.13, which the authors call modest and an association, not a mechanism.
claims.metric: mean rank difference, TimesFM family minus Chronos family
claims.dataset: weather, air quality, electricity, exchange rates pooled

claims.text: On hourly Danish electricity (46 load and generation series) the best pretrained model is 10.6% worse than Theta on mean MASE (Chronos-2 1.155, TimesFM 3 1.157, Theta 1.045); Theta ranks first and six models, pretrained ones included, are statistically tied with it.
claims.metric: mean MASE change, best pretrained vs best classical (%)
claims.dataset: Energinet Energi Data Service, hourly, 46 series

claims.text: On the electricity group the nominal 80% interval of TimesFM 3 covers 69% of outcomes (the pretrained models range from 62% to 69%), while Theta covers 86%.
claims.dataset: Energinet Energi Data Service, hourly, 46 series

claims.text: Seasonal strength and spectral entropy of the input window do not order the gains across the seven groups; the authors note that seven groups cannot support a correlation either way.

relevance.rationale: The headline is about Wikipedia pageviews and about how benchmarks are built, not about load. One of the seven groups is hourly electricity: 46 Danish settlement series that mix load and generation columns, with no load-only result, so the target is scored 2 rather than 3. Hourly groups are forecast 48 hours ahead from a single origin, which is closest to day-ahead on our scale (2) and far from our 168 hours over 52 origins. Every model runs on the series history alone, with no weather or other covariate, so covariates are scored 1. Its relevance to us is as a caveat on our 'weeks after weights' count: a later test window does not make a domain unfamiliar to the model.

checks.notes: Central model: the headline claim is about the TimesFM family on Wikipedia and its largest-gain cell belongs to TimesFM 3, so runnable_class, license and training_overlap_risk refer to google/timesfm-3.0-pytorch; Chronos-2 and TimesFM 2.5, which the study also ran, are in implementation_hint. training_overlap_risk: high. It is about our run: the weights file was committed on 2026-08-24 22:41 UTC (repository commit history, read through the Hugging Face API; later commits are titled README, LICENSE and metadata changes), so 10 of our 52 scored weeks (31 Aug to 2 Nov 2026) start after it, fewer than half. A finding of this run that bears on the paper itself: the paper states that every checkpoint, timesfm-3.0-pytorch included, was published before its 1 Jan 2026 origin, but that repository was created on 24 Aug 2026. For the model behind the largest gain, the premise 'test data dated after the release' therefore does not hold on the repository dates; the hourly and daily test windows (to mid-January), the weekly one (to about April) and nearly all of the monthly one (to August) end before the weights appeared. The card's stated data cutoff for Wikipedia pageviews (Nov 2023, from the research tool's copy of the card) would still put the 2026 test data outside the corpus, but that rests on the card, not on the release date the paper argues from. Whether an earlier TimesFM 3 checkpoint existed elsewhere before 2026 was not checked. pre_registered: no. The paper says series lists were fixed before results were seen, but no dated plan or registration exists, and the authors say they set out to find a series property and changed explanation after the results. independent_replication: unknown. One search and one research task found no rerun or critique with new numbers, only an automated review and an automated arXiv digest (neither fetched nor cited). evidence_strength: weak, by the window rule. Code and results folders are public and the baselines got the same inputs (same history, same 2,016-point cap, all univariate), but there is one forecast origin, and the test windows are 2 days for the three hourly groups and 14 days for the two daily ones; only weekly (91 days) and monthly Wikipedia (about 8 months) reach 90 days. No intervals are given for the headline numbers (ranks carry Nemenyi intervals in a figure only), so ci90 is empty. The familiarity result is modest (rank-biserial -0.13), rests on one corpus and one domain, and compares model families that differ in more than their corpora; the authors say so. Arithmetic check of Table 3 against Table 1: daily 25.8, weekly 28.4, monthly 16.9 and air quality 12.6 reproduce; weather comes to 12.4 (paper 12.5) and electricity to -10.5 (paper -10.6), consistent with rounding. Not verified: files in the repository were not opened (only the top page and two listings), so the per-series losses, the hold-out scripts and the lock file are unchecked, and the README describes an older M4/M3/Tourism benchmark, not this study; the paper's statement that TimesFM's authors describe Wikipedia pageviews as the bulk of the corpus (the two model cards list pageviews without shares; the TimesFM paper and Google's announcement were not read); the contents of the Chronos corpus (the research answer said it includes Wikipedia and load data, but no source text I saw backs that, so it is not used); the TimesFM 3 data list, which my own fetch of the card did not return and which is taken from the research tool's source list; the last part of the paper's reference list was not read (the rest of the full text was). Which of the 46 electricity series are load was not stated in the paper. Tools: one research task at the standard tier, one search, 9 pages fetched (none failed; one Hugging Face commits page came back without dates and the API listing was used instead).

label: PARTIAL
label_reason: A sourced study with public code, but its headline comparison (pretrained against classical methods across domains, and TimesFM against Chronos on Wikipedia versus elsewhere) cannot be re-measured on a one-domain load benchmark, and load enters only as part of a 46-series electricity group forecast 48 hours ahead from one origin without covariates. The evidence is thin by our rules (a 2-day window on the electricity group, no pre-registration, no replication), and the TimesFM 3 weights it relies on were uploaded in August 2026, after the hold-out origin the paper says they precede.
implementation_hint: Nothing to run as a receipt: the claim is a contrast between domains and our benchmark has one. The models themselves are ones we can run: google/timesfm-3.0-pytorch (central model, ff_native_exog through models_ff/run_ff.py; non-commercial weights, 10 of 52 scored weeks after the 2026-08-24 upload), amazon/chronos-2 (direct_adapter, models/chronos2.py) and google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch (ff_univariate, models_ff/run_ff.py); Chronos-Bolt and Moirai 2.0 would go through FoundationForecast as univariate. Use for us: (1) wording of receipts, where 'weeks after weights' should be read as ruling out seen observations, not as making hourly load an unfamiliar domain; (2) a secondary check already possible from existing rows: compare error ratios on weeks before and after each weights date, univariate rows included, to see whether the electricity result (no advantage over a simple classical method) appears at 168 hours on PJM; (3) the calibration finding (80% intervals covering 62 to 69% on electricity) is a reason to report coverage if quantiles are ever scored. The study's electricity baseline is Theta, not a temperature regression, and its horizon is 48 hours.
